Key Finding: Chess instruction may support learning, but measured transfer to academic and cognitive skills is modest and limited by study design.
APA Reference: Sala, G., & Gobet, F. (2016). Do the benefits of chess instruction transfer to academic and cognitive skills? A meta-analysis. Educational Research Review, 18, 46–57. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2016.02.002

Key Finding: A randomized trial in England found no effect of chess lessons on mathematics, reading, or science scores, cautioning against promising broad academic gains.
APA Reference: Jerrim, J., Macmillan, L., Micklewright, J., Sawtell, M., & Wiggins, M. (2018). Does teaching children how to play cognitively demanding games improve their educational attainment? Journal of Human Resources, 53(4), 993–1029. https://doi.org/10.3368/jhr.53.4.0516.7952R

Key Finding: UNESCO finds digital learning can extend access, but connectivity gaps leave many learners unable to benefit from online education.
APA Reference: Global Education Monitoring Report Team. (2023). Global education monitoring report 2023: Technology in education: A tool on whose terms? UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org/gem-report/en/technology

Key Finding: UNESCO recommends that education technology be adopted only when appropriate, equitable, evidence-based, and sustainable.
APA Reference: Global Education Monitoring Report Team. (2023). Global education monitoring report 2023: Technology in education: A tool on whose terms? UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org/gem-report/en/technology

Key Finding: UNESCO reports that short- and long-term costs of education technology are often underestimated, challenging assumptions that digital delivery is automatically cheaper.
APA Reference: Global Education Monitoring Report Team. (2023). Global education monitoring report 2023: Technology in education: A tool on whose terms? UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org/gem-report/en/technology

Key Finding: Affordable connectivity remains a policy priority, so data and device costs can limit the addressable market for a browser-based learning product.
Data centres consumed about 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, making hosting efficiency a relevant environmental consideration even for digital products.
APA Reference: International Energy Agency. (2025). Energy and AI: Energy demand from AI. https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai/energy-demand-from-ai

Key Finding: The UN digital compact calls for sustainability across the full life cycle of digital infrastructure and equipment.
The Global Digital Compact commits governments to closing digital divides and expanding meaningful, affordable connectivity.
The Compact calls for stronger frameworks to protect children online, making child-focused digital education a matter of policy as well as product design.
Under GDPR Article 8, services relying on consent for children’s data need parental authorization below the applicable national age threshold, which may be 13–16.
APA Reference: European Parliament and Council of the European Union. (2016). Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation), Article 8. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj

Key Finding: The Convention on the Rights of the Child protects children against arbitrary or unlawful interference with privacy and recognizes their right to education.
APA Reference: United Nations. (1989). Convention on the Rights of the Child. https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/crc.pdf

Key Finding: UNESCO says learner-facing AI must respect privacy and avoid using student interaction data for commercial exploitation; this supports keeping MVP learning records minimal.
APA Reference: UNESCO. (2021). Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. https://www.unesco.org/en/legal-affairs/recommendation-ethics-artificial-intelligence

Key Finding: UNESCO warns that education technology can deepen existing inequalities, so accessibility and low-bandwidth usability should be considered core product qualities.
APA Reference: Global Education Monitoring Report Team. (2023). Global education monitoring report 2023: Technology in education: A tool on whose terms? UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org/gem-report/en/technology
